item.title: Before You Colorize an Old Photo, Find Out What Color Things Really Were
item.content:encoded:
A colorized photo can feel like a window into the past, or it can feel like a costume. The difference is rarely the software. It is whether the colors are right: the car, the uniform, the wallpaper, the dress your great-grandmother wore to church. A few minutes of research before you colorize gets you a result your family will believe.

Here is how I look up real colors before touching a black and white photo.

A 1939 farmhouse in Malheur County, Oregon, before and after colorizing. The sedan came out dark green, a common factory color for cars of that era, but the make and year are what would settle it. Photo: Dorothea Lange, Library of Congress.

Start with what the photo already tells you

Black and white is not colorless information. Each color turns into its own shade of gray, so the photo still holds clues.

  • Very dark clothing in older portraits is often black, navy or dark brown. Bright red and royal blue usually come out as mid gray, not black.
  • A light shirt with a slight tone next to a pure white collar is probably cream or pale blue, not white.
  • Skies in old prints are often pale or almost white, because early film saw blue as light. Do not assume an overcast day.

Write down what you can rule out. It narrows every later choice.

Ask the people who were there

The best source is still a relative. Ask about one thing at a time, because "what colors were in this photo?" gets a shrug, while "what color was Grandpa's truck?" gets a story. Also look for color photos of the same people or places from a few years later. A house, a car or a favorite coat often shows up again.

Look up objects with a known color

Many things in old photos had standard colors you can check.

  • Cars: search the make, model and year with "paint colors" or "original colors". Manufacturer brochures and enthusiast clubs list the colors offered that year.
  • Uniforms: military, police, school and sports uniforms are well documented. Search the unit or team name with the year.
  • Signs and brands: store signs, packaging and logos were usually printed in brand colors. Old advertisements show them.
  • Buildings: churches, schools and town halls often still stand. A current street view photo is a good guide for brick and stone, less so for painted wood.

Use period references for everything else

When nothing is documented, aim for colors that were common at the time rather than colors that look good today.

  • Mail-order catalogs from the period show clothing and household colors, often with color plates.
  • Museum collections online let you browse clothing and objects by decade.
  • Hand-colored postcards of the same town show how people of the era imagined their own streets.

A postcard of Main Street, Danbury, Connecticut. Colored postcards like this show which car, awning and brick colors people of the time expected to see. Tichnor Brothers collection, Boston Public Library.

Earth tones, muted greens and dusty blues are safe guesses for many decades before the 1950s. Saturated, bright colors were less common and more expensive.

Colorize, then check it against your notes

Once you know what you are aiming for, the colorizing itself is the quick part. I run the scan through Clarpex's photo colorizer to get a natural starting point in under a minute, then compare the result with my notes. If the AI turned a navy uniform brown or painted a known red car blue, I fix those areas in a photo editor with a color layer set to the Color blend mode.

Two habits help:

  • Keep the original scan. Colorizing is an interpretation, so always save the black and white file next to the color one.
  • Write down what you know and what you guessed. A short caption like "truck color confirmed by Uncle Joe, dress color is a guess" keeps the photo honest for the next generation.

A quick checklist

  1. Note what the gray tones rule out.
  2. Ask relatives about specific objects.
  3. Look up cars, uniforms, signs and buildings.
  4. Use catalogs and museum collections for the rest.
  5. Colorize, compare with your notes, fix what is wrong.
  6. Save both versions and label what was guessed.

A colorized photo will never be a record of the day it was taken, but with a little research it can come close. And the research itself often turns up stories that are worth more than the colors.
